figures.caption: **Figure 1. Some materials barely matter. Some block a lot.** Wood, drywall and plain glass take little. Concrete takes much more. These are computed for one layer, head-on.
figures.alt: Figure 1. Some materials barely matter. Some block a lot. Wood, drywall and plain glass take little. Concrete takes much more. These are computed for one layer, head-on.

figures.caption: **Figure 2. Measured in a lab.** Same scale as Figure 1. Longer bars mean more signal lost.
figures.alt: Figure 2. Measured in a lab. Same scale as Figure 1. Longer bars mean more signal lost.

figures.caption: **Figure 3. A thin layer of metal sends the signal back outside.** It might be foil in the wall or a coating on the glass. What reaches the kitchen comes in through the gaps.
figures.alt: Figure 3. A thin layer of metal sends the signal back outside. It might be foil in the wall or a coating on the glass. What reaches the kitchen comes in through the gaps.

figures.caption: **Figure 4. A sealed house lets signal in only through its gaps.** Lime is the signal that gets in. Gray is the signal the coatings send back. Not to scale.
figures.alt: Figure 4. A sealed house lets signal in only through its gaps. Lime is the signal that gets in. Gray is the signal the coatings send back. Not to scale.

figures.caption: **Figure 5. Higher bands lose more through the wall.** The energy-efficient building (green) loses much more at the higher band on the right. The older building barely changes.
figures.alt: Figure 5. Higher bands lose more through the wall. The energy-efficient building (green) loses much more at the higher band on the right. The older building barely changes.

figures.caption: **Figure 6. The outdoor test decides it.** A booster needs signal outside to bring in. Wi-Fi Calling and a network extender don't.
figures.alt: Figure 6. The outdoor test decides it. A booster needs signal outside to bring in. Wi-Fi Calling and a network extender don't.

figures.caption: **Figure 7. Wi-Fi Calling goes around the walls.** The lime path is your call: over your Wi-Fi and your home internet to your carrier.
figures.alt: Figure 7. Wi-Fi Calling goes around the walls. The lime path is your call: over your Wi-Fi and your home internet to your carrier.

figures.caption: **Figure 8. Catch it outside, repeat it inside.** The outside antenna faces the tower. The amplifier makes the signal stronger. The inside antenna fills one part of the house.
figures.alt: Figure 8. Catch it outside, repeat it inside. The outside antenna faces the tower. The amplifier makes the signal stronger. The inside antenna fills one part of the house.

figures.caption: **Figure 9. Distance and walls keep them apart.** The gap between the two antennas has to block more than the booster adds.
figures.alt: Figure 9. Distance and walls keep them apart. The gap between the two antennas has to block more than the booster adds.

figures.caption: **Figure 10. Open air alone isn't enough.** The bar on the left is how much an all-carrier home booster may add. The others show how much distance takes away. Walls and the roof make up the rest.
figures.alt: Figure 10. Open air alone isn't enough. The bar on the left is how much an all-carrier home booster may add. The others show how much distance takes away. Walls and the roof make up the rest.

figures.caption: **Figure 11. Register first, then switch it on.** Your carrier has to know about a booster before it goes on the air.
figures.alt: Figure 11. Register first, then switch it on. Your carrier has to know about a booster before it goes on the air.

figures.caption: **Figure 12. Three ways into the same carrier.** Two ride your internet and ignore the walls. The booster rides the tower's own signal and needs some of it outside.
figures.alt: Figure 12. Three ways into the same carrier. Two ride your internet and ignore the walls. The booster rides the tower's own signal and needs some of it outside.
